sw-vibe-coding/sw-apl , 
sw-embed/sw-cor24-apl, 
sw-embed/web-sw-cor24-apl, and https://mlpl.softwarewrighter.com/ -- I'd like to consider a new approach to the intersection of APL and ML.  So imagine an APL2-inspired language (glyphs, right to left) that has ML primitives, new glyphs.  One approach would be to parse actual math expressions, which can be multi-line, with the notations above and below sums and products.  See also 
sw-vibe-coding/DiscoveryOne for ideas about parsing Espanso multiline expressions.  (secondary idea: how do tuples as first class language items fit in with an APL-like array language?).   I'm thinking of something like APLML (A Programming Language for Machine Learning) or just M or L in the style of A, J, K.    Also, there could be unicode-based glyphs for ML built-ins in sw-MLPL, like adam, relu, softmax, linear, sigmoid, etc.  --- With espanso, an escaped key stroke could produce a glyph and a smart editor could annotate glyphs with tooltips.  Help me come up with a design and plan for this idea.

You’re describing something more interesting than “APL with a few neural-network functions.” The coherent version is a new array language whose notation deliberately sits between APL and mathematical ML notation:

APL-style right-to-left evaluation and array semantics.
APL2-style nested arrays as the basis for structured data.
ML primitives that operate on whole tensors/models/parameter structures.
A second, spatial mathematical surface syntax for expressions such as sums, products, gradients, losses, and indexed tensor equations.
Tooling that makes glyph entry practical rather than nostalgic.

I would separate the idea into three layers, because trying to solve all of them in one grammar would likely make the language incoherent.

1. The core language: “APL for tensors”

The core should remain recognizably APL.

That matters because your current sw-apl already gives you the hard parts: a clean-room Rust interpreter, genuine glyph syntax, right-to-left evaluation, arbitrary-rank arrays, a browser implementation, Espanso/Emacs input, workspaces, and regression/conformance infrastructure. Its main historical limitation for this experiment is intentional: it models APL\360 / 5100-era APL rather than APL2, so it currently has flat arrays, no nesting, and no Each.

By contrast, sw-cor24-apl has already explored exactly two features that become important here: nested/boxed arrays and Each, while retaining a right-to-left recursive-descent parser.

That suggests:

Do not mutate historical sw-apl into ML-APL. Fork the semantic architecture and create a new language mode/project.

Call the research language M, L, or APLML; keep sw-apl historically disciplined.

My preference for the actual language name is M.

It fits the Iverson-family tradition:

A → J → K → … → M

and “M” can quietly stand for Machine, Model, Matrix, or ML, without making the language name cumbersome.

APLML would be the better descriptive repo name initially, though:

sw-aplml

with:

Language: M
Tagline: an array language for machine learning

That avoids trying to own an unsearchable one-letter repository.

2. Don't make relu, softmax, etc. merely funny spellings

This is the most important design decision.

Something like:

Y ← relu W+.×X

becoming:

Y ← ♢ W+.×X

doesn't really create a new language. It saves characters.

Instead, ML primitives should exploit APL-level semantics.

For example, classic APL already gives you a concise linear layer:

B + W +.× X

depending on axis convention.

So Linear does not necessarily deserve a primitive glyph at all. Its value is primarily as a parameterized/model object, not as a mathematical operator.

Likewise ReLU is already conceptually:

0⌈X

and sigmoid can be defined compositionally.

This gives you a useful rule:

A primitive earns a glyph only if it introduces a useful semantic concept that is awkward to express compositionally.

For example:

Concept	Existing array expression	New primitive justified?
ReLU	0⌈X	probably no
sigmoid	simple composition	probably no
softmax	possible but verbose + numerically subtle	yes
matmul	+.×	no
convolution	awkward axis/window expression	yes
gradient	impossible as ordinary array primitive	yes
loss	could be library function	maybe
optimizer step	stateful structural transform	yes
attention	composition of common ops	maybe library first
stop-gradient	new AD semantics	yes
parameter	new semantic category	yes
trainable model	structured value	yes

So rather than inventing twenty pictograms for PyTorch functions, create a small ML glyph vocabulary.

3. A proposed ML glyph vocabulary

Unicode already contains a very large mathematical operator repertoire, but Unicode explicitly does not assign unique semantics to every mathematical use; applications/languages decide those meanings in context.

That means you can use existing Unicode characters rather than inventing a custom font.

I would begin with about six new semantic primitives.

Glyph	Spoken form	Meaning
∇	grad	derivative / gradient
⨂	tensor	tensor/outer interaction, if not conflicting with APL outer product
⧉	window	sliding window / convolution operand
⌁	soft	normalize logits / softmax-like transform
⚿ or another safe glyph	param	trainable parameter
↻	step	optimizer state transition

I'm intentionally not strongly endorsing those exact glyphs yet. Glyph selection should come after the semantic inventory, because visually clever symbols become regrettable language syntax.

One especially good candidate is:

∇

because ML users already understand it.

Example:

G ← ∇ Loss Params

or, preserving stronger APL dyadic structure:

Params ∇ Loss

But I would actually treat ∇ as an operator, not a function:

∇Loss Params

meaning:

derive the gradient function of Loss, then apply it to Params.

That is much more Iversonian.

4. Operators are probably more important than new functions

This is where the language could become genuinely distinctive.

APL's superpower isn't merely arrays. It is that functions can be transformed by operators.

Machine learning is full of function transformations:

differentiate a function
vectorize a function
batch a function
checkpoint a function
jit/compile a function
map over devices
calculate value-and-gradient
attach trainable parameters
freeze part of a model

These map beautifully onto the APL operator concept.

For example, conceptually:

∇F

gradient of F

⌸F

batched/vectorized F

F¨

Each, already familiar from modern APL

F⍤R

rank-sensitive application

and potentially:

F⍢

training/update transformation

So an optimizer might not be:

adam(model, gradients)

but:

Params ← Rate Adam Loss Params

or even an operator-derived training verb:

Train ← Adam⍤Loss
Params ← Train Params Batch

The exact notation needs experimentation, but this direction is stronger than assigning Adam a decorative Unicode glyph.

5. The real breakthrough: make mathematical notation another surface syntax

Your multiline idea is potentially the differentiator.

Don't try to force two-dimensional mathematics directly into the ordinary APL lexer.

Instead build:

          ┌─────────────┐
APL glyph │             │
source ──▶│             │
          │ semantic IR │──▶ evaluator
Math 2D ─▶│             │
source    │             │
          └─────────────┘

APL syntax and mathematical notation are then two parsers for one expression IR.

That is very similar philosophically to what web-sw-cor24-apl already does in the other direction: it can display the same operations as representative ASCII words, APL glyphs, or literate descriptions.

You would extend that idea from display aliases to actual bidirectional notation.

6. Do not encode 2-D math as fake lines of text

For example, this:

$$ \operatorname{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}} {\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}} $$

cannot robustly be represented by counting spaces in:

              e^zᵢ
    ----------------------
        K
        Σ     e^zⱼ
       j=1

unless the editor owns the layout.

Unicode itself distinguishes between character encoding and higher-level mathematical composition; MathML/TeX-like systems provide structure that plain Unicode doesn't.

So I would borrow the best DiscoveryOne idea:

position is syntax, but serialize position explicitly.

DiscoveryOne already proposes source objects with (x,y,z) coordinates and semantic facets. You only need (x,y) for mathematics.

Internally:

struct MathGlyph {
    text: String,
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

but very quickly parse those into structural nodes:

Fraction
 ├─ numerator
 │   └─ Exp(Index(z,i))
 └─ denominator
     └─ Sum
         ├─ binder: j
         ├─ lower: 1
         ├─ upper: K
         └─ Exp(Index(z,j))

That becomes:

Expr::Div(
    Exp(Index(z,i)),
    Reduce {
        op: Add,
        binder: j,
        range: 1..K,
        body: Exp(Index(z,j))
    }
)

And then lower it to APL-array semantics.

That separation is crucial.

7. Math notation → array algebra should be visible

This would make an excellent teaching/research environment.

Input:

$$ y_i = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}} $$

Compiler interpretation:

index notation
      ↓
axis semantics
      ↓
array algebra
      ↓
M/APL source

For example, conceptually:

E ← * X - ⌈/X
Y ← E ÷ +/E

The user could switch among:

paper math
indexed math AST
APL/M expression
shape trace
evaluated arrays

That dovetails extremely well with what you're doing in MLPL and the “learn visually” direction.

And it gives the project an educational purpose larger than “APL with ML built-ins.”

8. Mathematical binders should be first-class compiler constructs

Sums and products are not merely glyphs.

This:

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i $$

contains:

operator      Σ
binder        i
lower bound   1
upper bound   n
body          x_i

So parse it initially as:

Reduce {
    op: Sum,
    variable: i,
    domain: Range(1,n),
    expr: x[i],
}

Then perform an arrayification pass.

If i indexes the only axis of x:

Σᵢ xᵢ

becomes:

+/X

For:

$$ y_i = \sum_j W_{ij}x_j $$

the compiler can recognize contraction:

contract axis j

and lower to an inner product / matrix-vector operation.

This would be an outstanding feature because users could see:

loops → indexed mathematics → contractions → array combinators

which is essentially the conceptual bridge between conventional ML notation and APL.

9. Add Einstein notation before adding dozens of ML built-ins

I'd prioritize this surprisingly highly.

For example:

$$ C_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik} B_{kj} $$

should become something structurally equivalent to:

C ← A +.× B

Likewise common tensor contractions could be inferred from repeated bound indices.

That means your language has something resembling:

math compiler
    ↓
index contraction
    ↓
APL array algebra

This is much more interesting than:

matmul(A,B)

And it fits your previous work translating CNN formulas to MLPL exceptionally well.

10. Tuples: yes—but don't confuse tuples with nested arrays

Your secondary question deserves a firm distinction.

APL2 already provides extremely powerful recursive heterogeneous structure: nested arrays may contain arrays of differing shape, rank, depth, and type.

So this:

(Weights Bias)

can already conceptually be represented as a nested array.

But a tuple should convey something different:

fixed-position product structure whose elements do not participate in ordinary array scalar extension/broadcasting as one homogeneous array.

For ML this matters greatly.

A layer may return:

(output, state)

An optimizer step may return:

(params, optimizer-state)

A training iteration might yield:

(loss, params, metrics)

Treating those as an ordinary nested vector is semantically weak.

So I would have three fundamental structural categories:

Scalar
Array
Tuple

with arrays recursively allowed to contain boxed/nested values if desired.

11. Make tuples named products, inspired by DiscoveryOne/Tuplet

DiscoveryOne's ancestry is relevant because Tuplet/DiscoveryOne treats named tuples and multi-output verbs as fundamental.

For M, I would simplify the idea.

For example:

R ← ⟨Loss Params Metrics⟩

or constructor syntax:

⟨loss: L, params: P, metrics: M⟩

and selection:

R.loss

You don't need to force tuple semantics into APL indexing.

The semantic distinction becomes:

Structure	Meaning
array	many things of the same structural axis space
nested array	array whose cells may themselves be arrays/objects
tuple	one product value consisting of distinct roles
named tuple	tuple with semantic fields

That distinction is extremely useful for ML.

Consider Adam state:

AdamState =
    ⟨step,
      first_moment,
      second_moment⟩

Those values are structurally related but are not an array.

12. Tuples solve a longstanding awkwardness in array languages

APL is excellent when one answer is an array.

Modern computation often wants multiple semantically different outputs.

Instead of conventions such as:

2⊃R

you could have:

R.params
R.loss

or destructuring:

⟨L P S⟩ ← Train Batch State

This would fit right-to-left evaluation nicely:

⟨Loss Params State⟩ ← Batch Train State

A function can remain conceptually monadic/dyadic yet return a product.

This is one place where I think departing from traditional APL is worth it.

13. A tentative core type model

I would avoid a traditional static type system initially.

Instead introduce structural runtime categories plus optional shape annotations:

Value
├── Scalar
│   ├── Int
│   ├── Float
│   ├── Complex
│   ├── Bool
│   └── Char
│
├── Array
│   ├── Shape
│   ├── Element storage
│   └── Rank
│
├── Box/Nested
│
├── Tuple
│   ├── positional
│   └── named
│
├── Function
│
└── Model/Parameter

Eventually:

Tensor[F32; B,H,W,C]

could exist as compiler metadata without infecting normal APL syntax.

14. Shape should be part of the language's explanatory model

APL already makes shape fundamental through ⍴.

ML should take that further.

For example a smart editor could show:

Y ← W +.× X

with hover metadata:

W : 768 × 3072
X : 3072 × 128
────────────────
Y : 768 × 128

And math notation:

$$ Y_{ij}=\sum_k W_{ik}X_{kj} $$

could annotate:

i → 768
j → 128
k → 3072 (contracted)

This may be more valuable pedagogically than the ML glyphs themselves.

15. The editor is part of the language

APL historically required specialized input.

You've already solved much of that problem in sw-apl: the browser has an APL keyboard, and the project explicitly supports Espanso and Emacs keymaps.

For M I would make this a first-class design principle:

Source remains Unicode text, but editing is mnemonic.

Example Espanso mappings:

\grad     → ∇
\rho      → ⍴
\iota     → ⍳
\each     → ¨
\sum      → ∑
\product  → ∏
\alpha    → α
\partial  → ∂

Maybe use an APL-style prefix key:

Alt-G G   → ∇
Alt-G R   → ⍴

but Espanso provides the portable baseline.

The editor should then display:

∇
Gradient operator
Derives a function computing ∂output/∂argument

on hover.

That largely eliminates the classic “APL hieroglyphics” objection.

16. Make glyphs readable without changing source

Borrow directly from web-sw-cor24-apl.

It already supports:

representative syntax
APL glyph syntax
literate syntax

Extend that to four synchronized views:

Glyph
    ∇Loss P

Mnemonic
    grad Loss P

Literate
    gradient-of Loss applied-to P

Mathematical
       ∂ Loss
    ─────────
       ∂ P

All four views point at the same AST.

That is a much stronger UI than a syntax highlighter.

17. Don't parse arbitrary printed mathematics in M0

There is a large difference between:

“our editor understands structured two-dimensional math”

and:

“paste arbitrary mathematics from a paper and we'll parse it.”

The latter rapidly becomes an OCR/TeX/CAS research project.

For the first version, constrain the grammar to:

fractions
superscripts
subscripts
Σ
Π
∂
∇
parentheses/brackets
indexed variables
equality
common arithmetic
perhaps expectation E
tensor contractions

That is enough for a surprisingly large fraction of introductory ML equations.

Softmax alone is a good proof:

$$ \sigma_i(z)=\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}} $$

Google's ML material uses essentially this standard formula.

18. The first demonstration should be softmax

It exercises nearly everything you care about.

Start with the paper notation:

$$ s_i = \frac{e^{z_i}} {\sum_j e^{z_j}} $$

Then show its interpretation:

numerator
    exponent(index(z,i))

denominator
    reduce(add, j, exponent(index(z,j)))

Then arrayify:

E ← *Z
S ← E ÷ +/E

Then stabilized version:

E ← *Z-⌈/Z
S ← E÷+/E

Then replace the implementation with a primitive if desired:

S ← ⌁Z

Clicking ⌁ could expand back into its definition.

That gives you a beautiful distinction between:

primitive as abstraction

and

array expression as explanation

19. Second demo: a linear layer should deliberately have no glyph

Math:

$$ y = Wx+b $$

M:

Y ← B + W +.× X

This demonstrates the opposite lesson:

APL already is an ML notation when the operation is fundamentally array algebra.

That's important intellectually. Otherwise the project risks seeming like a Unicode façade over a tensor library.

20. Third demo: gradient descent

Math:

$$ \theta_{t+1} = \theta_t-\eta\nabla_\theta L(\theta_t) $$

M might look like:

Θ ← Θ - η × ∇Loss Θ

That is where the ML extension pays for itself.

And then:

Train ← {
    Θ ← Θ - η × ∇Loss Θ
}

or an eventual derived optimizer form.

21. Fourth demo: Adam shows why tuples matter

Adam has:

parameters
first moment
second moment
step
hyperparameters

So something like:

State ← ⟨step:0 m:0×Θ v:0×Θ⟩

then:

⟨Θ State⟩ ← Grad AdamStep ⟨Θ State⟩

This makes the tuple work clearly justified rather than an arbitrary language feature.

22. Fifth demo: CNN equation → array operation

Use one of the nested-sum convolution equations you've been exploring.

Something like:

$$ Y_{i,j,k} = \sum_m\sum_n\sum_c X_{i+m,j+n,c}K_{m,n,c,k} $$

Your math parser recognizes:

free indices:      i j k
contracted:        m n c

and lowers it to:

window + contraction

Then either:

Y ← K Conv X

or a composition of window and inner-product primitives.

This would connect directly to the CNN/math work in MLPL.

23. Architecture

I'd build the research implementation in Rust and reuse your established pattern:

                     ┌───────────────┐
Unicode APL/M ──────▶│ glyph parser  │
                     └──────┬────────┘
                            │
2D math editor ─────────────┤
                     ┌──────▼────────┐
                     │ semantic AST  │
                     └──────┬────────┘
                            │
                   ┌────────▼────────┐
                   │ shape/index IR  │
                   └────────┬────────┘
                            │
                 ┌──────────▼─────────┐
                 │ arrayification pass │
                 └──────────┬─────────┘
                            │
                    ┌───────▼───────┐
                    │ array/ML IR   │
                    └───┬───────┬───┘
                        │       │
                  interpreter  MLPL?
                        │       │
                       WASM   teaching view

I would not compile math text straight to executable operations.

Keep the intermediate index representation visible and testable.

24. Five small Rust components

This also fits your preferred project-size discipline reasonably well.

m-core
    Value, Array, Tuple, Shape

m-parse
    traditional glyph parser

m-math
    spatial math parser + indexed-expression IR

m-lower
    index analysis + arrayification

m-eval
    evaluator + AD primitives

Then:

m-web

as a separate app consuming those.

sw-apl itself remains untouched except perhaps extracting/reusing ideas or small libraries where sensible.

25. Autodiff should be phase 2, but architect for it immediately

If ∇ is going to mean anything beyond symbolic rewriting, every primitive eventually needs derivative metadata.

For instance:

Primitive {
    eval
    shape_rule
    derivative_rule
}

Conceptually:

Add
  eval:       x+y
  shape:      broadcast(x,y)
  derivative: (dx,dy) → dx+dy

This gives you:

evaluation
shape inference
automatic differentiation
documentation

from the same primitive registry.

That registry could be the heart of the language.

26. I'd make primitives declarative

For example, conceptually:

primitive softmax {
    glyph:    "⌁"
    name:     "softmax"
    arity:    1
    rank:     last-axis
    shape:    identity
    expand:   exp(x-max(x)) / sum(exp(x-max(x)))
    grad:     ...
}

Then the browser can generate:

tooltip
help
mnemonic entry
pretty rendering
shape rule
expansion
tests

from one definition.

This would be a good evolution beyond both current APL implementations.

27. MLPL and M should remain different languages

I would resist merging the two.

They serve different pedagogical purposes.

MLPL
Readable
word-oriented
explicit
good for stepping through concepts
approachable
M
dense
symbolic
array-first
close to mathematical notation
composition-oriented

They can share the semantic ML layer.

For example:

MLPL:
softmax logits

M:
⌁Z

Math:
        eᶻⁱ
──────────────────
   Σⱼ eᶻʲ

All could lower to something like:

MlOp::Softmax(axis=-1)

That creates an unexpectedly useful architecture:

MLPL and M become two experimental languages over the same ML semantics.

28. In fact, build the shared IR first

I would create something like:

enum Expr {
    Scalar(...),
    Array(...),
    Tuple(Vec<Expr>),
    NamedTuple(...),

    Apply(...),
    Reduce(...),
    Contract(...),
    Index(...),

    Grad(...),
    StopGrad(...),
    Parameter(...),
}

Then:

MLPL ───┐
        ├──▶ ML IR
M ──────┤
        │
Math ───┘

This gives you a very clean research story.

29. Suggested roadmap

I would make the first milestones deliberately small.

Milestone	Result
M0	fork/minimal glyph APL evaluator with nested arrays + Each
M1	first-class positional and named tuples
M2	shape-aware expression IR
M3	paper-math editor for Σ, indices, fraction, exponent
M4	index-expression lowering to reductions/contractions
M5	softmax math → M expression → execution
M6	∇ + reverse-mode autodiff
M7	linear regression trained entirely in M
M8	optimizer state + Adam + named tuples
M9	convolution/index-sum demo
M10	synchronized Math / Glyph / Mnemonic / Literate views
M11	bridge selected expressions to/from MLPL
Definition of a convincing M5 demo

A user should be able to enter:

       eᶻⁱ
────────────────
    Σ  eᶻʲ
     j

and watch it become:

indexed IR
      ↓
reduction IR
      ↓
E ← *Z-⌈/Z
E÷+/E
      ↓
[0.0900 0.2447 0.6652]

That alone is a publishable-quality project demo.

30. One UI I would build

Not a notebook clone.

A four-pane “notation microscope”:

┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
│ PAPER                │ M                    │
│                      │                      │
│      eᶻⁱ             │ E←*Z-⌈/Z            │
│ ─────────────        │ E÷+/E                │
│    Σⱼ eᶻʲ           │                      │
├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ STRUCTURE            │ RESULT / SHAPES      │
│                      │                      │
│ Divide               │ Z   [3]              │
│ ├ Exp(Index z i)     │ E   [3]              │
│ └ Sum j              │ out [3]              │
│   └ Exp(Index z j)   │ .09 .24 .67          │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

Click Σ and the relevant +/ highlights.

Click j, and the reduced axis highlights.

Click the denominator, and the actual intermediate array appears.

That ties together APL, ML, mathematics, and your microscope-style explanatory work unusually well.

31. What I would not do

Avoid these early:

40 new ML glyphs.
GPU support.
full PyTorch compatibility.
general symbolic algebra.
arbitrary LaTeX import.
arbitrary handwritten/pasted math recognition.
static dependent tensor types.
trying to run existing Python models.
modifying historical sw-apl semantics.
giving every named ML function a primitive.

Those are distractions from the distinctive idea.

The research question should instead be:

Can mathematical ML notation be mechanically transformed into concise array-language programs, while retaining an executable connection between the notation, shapes, intermediate arrays, and learning process?

That is a crisp and unusual project.

32. The language identity I'd use

My naming stack would currently be:

Project/repository
    sw-aplml

Language
    M

Expanded name
    M — A Programming Language for Machine Learning

Heritage
    APL2-inspired array semantics
    Iverson notation
    modern tensor computation

There is a nice historical joke hidden there:

APL = A Programming Language
M = Machine Learning, written as an array language

And the front-page program should probably not be “Hello World.” It should be:

$$ y_i=\frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}} $$

next to:

E←*X-⌈/X
Y←E÷+/E

with both executing to the same result.

That immediately communicates why this project exists.

The three ideas I would prototype first
APL2-ish nested arrays + named tuples on top of the modern Rust interpreter architecture.
A structured 2-D sum/index parser, narrowly constrained to indexed sums and fractions.
One shared semantic IR that both M and MLPL can target.

If those three work, then ∇, Adam, convolution, attention, and richer mathematical notation have a very solid place to grow into.

continue, you stopped mid-diagram (again)

              SOURCE REPRESENTATIONS
         ┌─────────┬──────────┬─────────┐

- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch.

`demo-decision-model` builds a tiny non-generative **Typed Decision Model (TDM)**

### What this repository is about

The subject is three primitives plus one capability: **Choice**, **Noul**,

### 2. BEGIN — `agentrail begin`
Run immediately after reading `next` output. This transitions the step from
Pending to InProgress so the recorded history matches what actually
happened.

### 3. WORK
Do what the step prompt says. Do NOT ask the user "want me to proceed?" or
"shall I start?" — the step prompt IS your instruction. Execute it.

### 4. COMMIT
Commit your code changes with git BEFORE running `agentrail complete`.
The commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at
the moment of `complete`, so the commit must land first.

### 5. COMPLETE — `agentrail complete`
```
agentrail complete --summary "what you accomplished" \
  --reward 1 \
  --actions "tools and approach used"
```
On failure: `--reward -1 --failure-mode "what went wrong"`.
On final step: add `--done`.

### 6. STOP
After `complete`, do NOT make further code changes. Anything after
`complete` is untracked and invisible to the next session. If you see more
work to do, it belongs in the NEXT step, not this one.

## Agentrail metadata discipline

When using agentrail, changes to `.agentrail/` files are first-class project
changes — the same as application source code. They must be committed, and
should be pushed before you hand off.

Before running `agentrail complete`:

1. `git status` — confirm `.agentrail/` files are tracked, not just present.
   Untracked files in `.agentrail/` mean the next session will not see them.
2. Stage and commit source changes and `.agentrail/` metadata together. The
   commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at the
   moment of `agentrail complete`, so the commit must happen *first*.
3. Run `agentrail complete` after the commit lands.
4. Push the branch (or note the unpushed branch state in your handoff).

This is the most common agentrail failure mode: agents do the work, commit
the source, and forget the `.agentrail/` files. The result is a saga whose
recorded history disagrees with git history, which `agentrail audit` will
flag — but only after the damage is done.

### What's hand-editable in `.agentrail/`

Three categories of files live here, and the rules differ:

- **Append-only saga state** — `saga.toml`, `step.toml`, `plan.md`, session
  JSONLs under `sessions/`, trajectory JSONs under `trajectories/`, and
  anything under `.agentrail-archive/`. **Never hand-edit or delete these.**
  They are written by agentrail commands and represent the durable saga
  record; hand-editing desyncs the saga from git history and from prior
  session memory. A direct `rm` on untracked files is unrecoverable.
- **Regenerated state** — `instruction-lock.toml`. Don't hand-edit; it is
  rewritten on every `agentrail instructions apply`, so any local changes
  are overwritten silently.
- **User config** — `instruction-profile.toml`. This is normal user-edited
  config, like `.gitconfig` or a `package.json`. Hand-edit it freely, or
  use `agentrail instructions profile *` subcommands to mutate via
  commands (which validate field values and surface typos).

## Working a branch in parallel with another agent

If another agent is working this same repo on its own branch at the same
time, you are both writing into `.agentrail/`. Step numbers are
per-branch and *will* collide — you will both have a `003-` — so your
step directories land on identical paths and the merge conflicts. The
**slug** is the only part that can keep the two lanes apart.

Pick a lane prefix naming your slice of the work (`rtx5060`, `rtx3060`,
`api`, `ui`) and namespace your saga with it:

```bash
agentrail rename prefix <lane> --dry-run   # preview, changes nothing
agentrail rename prefix <lane>             # apply
git add -A .agentrail/                     # -A: a dir move is a delete + an add
git commit -m "saga: rename into <lane> lane"
```

... [5210 characters truncated] ...

entrail audit`

Compares first-parent git history against saga steps and reports gaps.
Default output is a markdown report; `--emit-commands` prints a shell
script of `agentrail add` lines pre-seeded from commit subjects:

```bash
agentrail audit                    # human-readable report
agentrail audit --emit-commands    # draft script (review before running)
agentrail audit --since HEAD~50    # limit scope
```

The emitted script is a draft — slugs and prompts come from commit
subjects and usually need rewording. Review and edit before executing.

### `agentrail snapshot` (belt-and-suspenders)

Captures `.agentrail/` (and `.agentrail-archive/` if present) into a real
git commit under `refs/agentrail/snapshots/<timestamp>`. The blobs are
reachable, survive `git gc`, and can be restored with a normal git
command:

```bash
agentrail snapshot                 # take a snapshot now
agentrail snapshot --list          # list existing refs
git restore --source=<ref> -- .agentrail .agentrail-archive
```

Run a snapshot before risky agent operations or after creating files
you haven't yet staged. It does NOT replace normal git tracking — it is
a safety net for what is not yet committed.

## Git hygiene

- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch.
- Never use `--no-verify` to skip pre-commit hooks unless explicitly told to.
  If a hook fails, fix the underlying issue.
- Prefer naming files explicitly (`git add path/to/file`) over `git add -A`,
  to avoid sweeping in unintended files (secrets, local scratch, etc.).
- Resolve merge conflicts; do not discard changes by default.

This file gives Claude Code (and other agentrail-aware agents) the rules for this project. The block below the H1 marked as `agentrail:global` is auto-managed by `agentrail instructions apply` — content outside those markers is preserved verbatim.

## Project-specific notes

`demo-decision-model` builds a tiny non-generative **Typed Decision Model (TDM)**
in sw-MLPL, plus the Rust/Yew/WASM microscope that shows it working.
[`docs/plan.md`](docs/plan.md) is the delivery plan and the authority for scope;
[`docs/research.txt`](docs/research.txt) is the source discussion.

### What this repository is about

The subject is three primitives plus one capability: **Choice**, **Noul**,
**Scale**, and **Memory**. ELIZA is **demo 01** — a forcing function and a free
deterministic oracle, not the point. Demo 02 (campus navigation) must run with
`lib/` unchanged; that is the test of whether the abstractions are real.

### Rules that are enforced, not merely intended

- **No generation path, ever.** There is no `generate(prompt) -> String`. Every
  string a user sees is exactly one of the candidates the program offered the
  model — either the composed candidate a Choice selected, or a committed frame
  with deterministically retrieved text spliced in. The model ranks; it never
  composes. A gate test asserts this in whichever form the turn used.
- **No demo identifiers in `lib/` or `crates/`.** `lib/` knows about decisions;
  `demos/eliza/` knows about ELIZA; the Rust crates know about traces. Checked
  by script.
- **Thresholds and side effects live in MLPL, never in the model.** The model
  reports belief; the program decides what to do about it.
- **Never call this a System One Model, and never claim it reproduces Jev.** We
  reproduce the published behavioral contract and the calibration objective. Our
  calibration stage is "calibration fine-tuning", not RLCD.
- **No accuracy claim without its per-category breakdown, its calibration
  numbers, and its margin over the `MB01` matcher on the same split.**
- **Never trust a teacher's stated confidence.** Soft labels come from Ollama
  first-token `top_logprobs`, renormalized over the legal answer set.

### Closing every step

After each planning, implementation, feature, or fix step:

1. Run **all** pre-commit checks, including the mlplunit tests (`just check`
   once it exists) — not just formatting and lint.
2. Commit to `main` with a detailed message.
3. Push.
4. Summarize what was pushed, the next step(s), any choices that need a
   decision, and any blockers found.

This project commits to `main` directly; the `feat/` to `pr/` branch-handoff
convention in the briefing above does not apply here unless asked for.

### Toolchain

- the adjacent [`../sw-mlpl`](https://github.com/sw-ml-study/sw-mlpl) checkout
  built in release mode (`target/release/mlpl-repl`), or an absolute `MLPL`
  override; measured against `mlpl-repl 0.22.0`;
- `mlplunit` on `PATH`, an absolute `MLPLUNIT` override, or the adjacent
  `../../softwarewrighter/mlplunit/bin/mlplunit` checkout;
- [`just`](https://github.com/casey/just);
- a Rust toolchain with the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target and `trunk`, for the
  microscope crates;
- [`ollama`](https://ollama.com) for the offline teacher track (Saga 7 only;
  every other lesson runs without it).

  3. View results:    reg-rs report -p my_test -v

  2. Use 'reg-rs run' to verify that changes haven't introduced regressions.
  3. Use 'reg-rs status' for real-time monitoring of long-running test suites.
  4. Always address failures before committing code.

  remove    Removes test database files matching a pattern

  help      Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

  -d, --debug

# demo-extensions

`demo-extensions` explores how independently built Rust libraries can add
native capabilities to the [sw-MLPL repository](https://github.com/sw-ml-study/sw-mlpl)
without adding each domain to the language runtime. Try the core language in
the [sw-MLPL playground](https://sw-ml-study.github.io/sw-mlpl/). This repository
now includes the original headless `hello` extension foundation plus native
interactive line-rendered applications, bounded model/media/filesystem
demonstrations, and a Rust/Yew ML microscope.

The wireframe cube remains the smallest visual teaching path. All interactive
native demos now initialize one retained scene, use stable-ID patches for
geometry/style changes, and use view updates for camera/help/status changes.

The repository proves the downstream extension boundary with a real
`.dylib`/`.so` and a Rust host harness. sw-MLPL now exposes a separate static
scalar registry plus a byte-compatible C-descriptor adapter: both its built-in
`hello:answer()` and this repository's `_hello:answer()` provider are proven
through the interpreter. Arrays, persistent handles, and nested records are now
also proven through the real downstream descriptor. `use hello`, compilation,
dynamic loading and compiled-provider startup remain tracked contracts.

## What is here

```text
crates/mlpl-extension-abi/      Versioned C-compatible ABI and validation
crates/mlpl-extension-loader/   Package resolver, dynamic loader, and registry
crates/mlpl-extension-sdk/      Safe author-facing SDK scaffold
crates/mlpl-http-contract/       Shared HTTP middleware policy validation
crates/mlpl-native3d-scene/      Generic line/point scenes and headless planning
lib/native3d/                    Reusable MLPL camera, picking, geometry, app loop
demos/wireframe-cube/            MLPL-owned bulk-array cube scene
demos/tic-tac-toe/               MLPL rules, minimax, and generic line scene
demos/life-plane/                 MLPL finite-grid Life model and presets
extensions/hello/               Rust cdylib, package manifest, and MLPL facade
extensions/digest/              Generic streaming SHA-256 over bytes and confined files
extensions/hftok/               Hugging Face byte-level BPE tokenizer with NFC and typed handles
extensions/http-client/         Bounded HTTP/HTTPS, verified large download, and middleware policy
extensions/http-server/         Callback-free bounded local HTTP server provider
extensions/sqlite/              Confined parameterized SQLite provider
extensions/boundary-probe/      Public-SDK array/handle/record host probe
extensions/canvas/              Dynamically loaded blocking winit/wgpu canvas
extensions/native3d/            Generic headless viewer and bulk line provider
tests/                          Native mlplunit and structural tests
docs/                           Architecture, contracts, plans, and evidence
```

The hello package demonstrates the intended separation:

- Rust exports private `_hello.answer`, `_hello.fail`, and `_hello.panic`
  functions through one `sw_mlpl_extension_v1` entry point.
- `extension.toml` selects an exact macOS or Linux native artifact and declares
  the public `hello` package separately from the private `_hello` namespace.
- `module.mlpl` is the public MLPL facade. It is tested as ordinary MLPL today
  and will bind to the native namespace once sw-MLPL provides the host hook.

## Prerequisites

For Qwen3 tokenization and pinned model downloads, see the
[Linux tokenizer and downloader delivery](docs/reasoning-linux-delivery.md)
for package paths, build commands, and measured compatibility, and the
[reasoning extensions acceptance report](docs/reasoning-extensions-acceptance.md)
for parity, throughput, and remaining upstream gates.

- Rust 1.85 or newer.
- [`just`](https://github.com/casey/just) for repository task aliases.
- The adjacent `../sw-mlpl` checkout with `target/release/mlpl-repl` or
  `target/debug/mlpl-repl`, or an absolute `MLPL` override.
- `mlplunit` on `PATH`, an absolute `MLPLUNIT` override, or the adjacent
  `/Users/mike/github/softwarewrighter/mlplunit/bin/mlplunit` checkout used by
  the project scripts.

The scripts only select existing tools; they never install or overwrite them.
Environment overrides must be absolute paths.

Open the smallest stock-interpreter graphical extension demo:

```sh
just array-canvas
```

MLPL computes a 720-point colored spiral, dynamically loads the separately
built canvas `.dylib`/`.so`, and blocks in one generic native presentation call
until the window closes. No custom evaluator host or injected Port is used. See
[Dynamic Array Canvas](docs/canvas-extension.md).

Start the persistent MLPL TodoMVC browser application:

```sh
just todomvc-server
# Browse to http://localhost:3000/ (http://127.0.0.1:3000/ also works)
```

The server-rendered page identifies itself as **sw-MLPL Demo: TodoMVC** and
links back to this repository and its MIT license directly from the interface.

The first start creates `var/todomvc/todos.sqlite3` and its `todos` table;
later starts retain the same rows. Set `TODOMVC_PORT`, `TODOMVC_DATA_DIR`
(absolute), or `TODOMVC_DB_NAME` (confined relative path) to override the
defaults. Stop with Control-C. `just todomvc-reset` drops the table explicitly;
the next start recreates it empty. `just todomvc` remains the no-server HTML
preview. See [MLPL web framework and TodoMVC](docs/mlpl-web-framework.md).

Run the executable MLPL HTTP-client demo through the real Rust provider:

```sh
just http-client
# or: just http-client https://example.com/
```

The default `https://time.gov/` request is an opt-in live-network example, not
a test dependency. The mandatory test runs the same
[`get.mlpl`](demos/http-client/get.mlpl) source against loopback.

Large artifacts use a separate bounded path that streams into a temporary file,
verifies a pinned size and SHA-256, and only then renames the result into
place:

```sh
just fetch-artifact URL EXPECTED_BYTES SHA256 RELATIVE_PATH
```

It writes beneath the git-ignored `models/` directory, reuses an already
verified file without opening a connection, and leaves nothing behind when a
transfer is truncated or tampered with. See the
[network/database extension plan](docs/network-db-extensions.md) for bounds,
the full request-record contract, and the error taxonomy.

## Build and test

Build the workspace and the independently loadable hello library:

```sh
cargo build --workspace
cargo build -p mlpl-extension-hello
```

Open the interactive native cube:

```sh
just cube-3d
```

Open the playable native tic-tac-toe game:

```sh
just tic-tac-toe
```

Open the editable native Life plane:

# demo-extensions

`demo-extensions` explores how independently built Rust libraries can add
native capabilities to the [sw-MLPL repository](https://github.com/sw-ml-study/sw-mlpl)
without adding each domain to the language runtime. Try the core language in
the [sw-MLPL playground](https://sw-ml-study.github.io/sw-mlpl/). This repository
now includes the original headless `hello` extension foundation plus native
interactive line-rendered applications, bounded model/media/filesystem
demonstrations, and a Rust/Yew ML microscope.

The wireframe cube remains the smallest visual teaching path. All interactive
native demos now initialize one retained scene, use stable-ID patches for
geometry/style changes, and use view updates for camera/help/status changes.

The repository proves the downstream extension boundary with a real
`.dylib`/`.so` and a Rust host harness. sw-MLPL now exposes a separate static
scalar registry plus a byte-compatible C-descriptor adapter: both its built-in
`hello:answer()` and this repository's `_hello:answer()` provider are proven
through the interpreter. Arrays, persistent handles, and nested records are now
also proven through the real downstream descriptor. `use hello`, compilation,
dynamic loading and compiled-provider startup remain tracked contracts.

## What is here

```text
crates/mlpl-extension-abi/      Versioned C-compatible ABI and validation
crates/mlpl-extension-loader/   Package resolver, dynamic loader, and registry
crates/mlpl-extension-sdk/      Safe author-facing SDK scaffold
crates/mlpl-http-contract/       Shared HTTP middleware policy validation
crates/mlpl-native3d-scene/      Generic line/point scenes and headless planning
lib/native3d/                    Reusable MLPL camera, picking, geometry, app loop
demos/wireframe-cube/            MLPL-owned bulk-array cube scene
demos/tic-tac-toe/               MLPL rules, minimax, and generic line scene
demos/life-plane/                 MLPL finite-grid Life model and presets
extensions/hello/               Rust cdylib, package manifest, and MLPL facade
extensions/digest/              Generic streaming SHA-256 over bytes and confined files
extensions/hftok/               Hugging Face byte-level BPE tokenizer with NFC and typed handles
extensions/http-client/         Bounded HTTP/HTTPS, verified large download, and middleware policy
extensions/http-server/         Callback-free bounded local HTTP server provider
extensions/sqlite/              Confined parameterized SQLite provider
extensions/boundary-probe/      Public-SDK array/handle/record host probe
extensions/canvas/              Dynamically loaded blocking winit/wgpu canvas
extensions/native3d/            Generic headless viewer and bulk line provider
tests/                          Native mlplunit and structural tests
docs/                           Architecture, contracts, plans, and evidence
```

The hello package demonstrates the intended separation:

- Rust exports private `_hello.answer`, `_hello.fail`, and `_hello.panic`
  functions through one `sw_mlpl_extension_v1` entry point.
- `extension.toml` selects an exact macOS or Linux native artifact and declares
  the public `hello` package separately from the private `_hello` namespace.
- `module.mlpl` is the public MLPL facade. It is tested as ordinary MLPL today
  and will bind to the native namespace once sw-MLPL provides the host hook.

## Prerequisites

For Qwen3 tokenization and pinned model downloads, see the
[Linux tokenizer and downloader delivery](docs/reasoning-linux-delivery.md)
for package paths, build commands, and measured compatibility, and the
[reasoning extensions acceptance report](docs/reasoning-extensions-acceptance.md)
for parity, throughput, and remaining upstream gates.

- Rust 1.85 or newer.
- [`just`](https://github.com/casey/just) for repository task aliases.
- The adjacent `../sw-mlpl` checkout with `target/release/mlpl-repl` or
  `target/debug/mlpl-repl`, or an absolute `MLPL` override.
- `mlplunit` on `PATH`, an absolute `MLPLUNIT` override, or the adjacent
  `/Users/mike/github/softwarewrighter/mlplunit/bin/mlplunit` checkout used by
  the project scripts.

The scripts only select existing tools; they never install or overwrite them.
Environment overrides must be absolute paths.

Open the smallest stock-interpreter graphical extension demo:

```sh
just array-canvas
```

MLPL computes a 720-point colored spiral, dynamically loads the separately
built canvas `.dylib`/`.so`, and blocks in one generic native presentation call
until the window closes. No custom evaluator host or injected Port is used. See
[Dynamic Array Canvas](docs/canvas-extension.md).

Start the persistent MLPL TodoMVC browser application:

```sh
just todomvc-server
# Browse to http://localhost:3000/ (http://127.0.0.1:3000/ also works)
```

The server-rendered page identifies itself as **sw-MLPL Demo: TodoMVC** and
links back to this repository and its MIT license directly from the interface.

The first start creates `var/todomvc/todos.sqlite3` and its `todos` table;
later starts retain the same rows. Set `TODOMVC_PORT`, `TODOMVC_DATA_DIR`
(absolute), or `TODOMVC_DB_NAME` (confined relative path) to override the
defaults. Stop with Control-C. `just todomvc-reset` drops the table explicitly;
the next start recreates it empty. `just todomvc` remains the no-server HTML
preview. See [MLPL web framework and TodoMVC](docs/mlpl-web-framework.md).

Run the executable MLPL HTTP-client demo through the real Rust provider:

```sh
just http-client
# or: just http-client https://example.com/
```

The default `https://time.gov/` request is an opt-in live-network example, not
a test dependency. The mandatory test runs the same
[`get.mlpl`](demos/http-client/get.mlpl) source against loopback.

Large artifacts use a separate bounded path that streams into a temporary file,
verifies a pinned size and SHA-256, and only then renames the result into
place:

```sh
just fetch-artifact URL EXPECTED_BYTES SHA256 RELATIVE_PATH
```

It writes beneath the git-ignored `models/` directory, reuses an already
verified file without opening a connection, and leaves nothing behind when a
transfer is truncated or tampered with. See the
[network/database extension plan](docs/network-db-extensions.md) for bounds,
the full request-record contract, and the error taxonomy.

Build the workspace and the independently loadable hello library:

```sh
cargo build --workspace
cargo build -p mlpl-extension-hello
```

Open the interactive native cube:

```sh
just cube-3d
```

Open the playable native tic-tac-toe game:

```sh
just tic-tac-toe
```

1	given my APL-related work: 
2	sw-vibe-coding/sw-apl ,

So imagine an APL2-inspired language (glyphs, right to left) that has ML primitives, new glyphs.  One approach would be to parse actual math expressions, which can be multi-line, with the notations above and below sums and products.  See also 
5	sw-vibe-coding/DiscoveryOne for ideas about parsing Espanso multiline expressions.  (secondary idea: how do tuples as first class language items fit in with an APL-like array language?).   I'm thinking of something like APLML (A Programming Language for Machine Learning) or just M or L in the style of A, J, K.    Also, there could be unicode-based glyphs for ML built-ins in sw-MLPL, like adam, relu, softmax, linear, sigmoid, etc.  --- With espanso, an escaped key stroke could produce a glyph and a smart editor could annotate glyphs with tooltips.  Help me come up with a design and plan for this idea.
6	
7	You’re describing something more interesting than “APL with a few neural-network functions.” The coherent version is a new array language whose notation deliberately sits between APL and mathematical ML notation:
8	
9	APL-style right-to-left evaluation and array semantics.
10	APL2-style nested arrays as the basis for structured data.
11	ML primitives that operate on whole tensors/models/parameter structures.
12	A second, spatial mathematical surface syntax for expressions such as sums, products, gradients, losses, and indexed tensor equations.
13	Tooling that makes glyph entry practical rather than nostalgic.
14	
15	I would separate the idea into three layers, because trying to solve all of them in one grammar would likely make the language incoherent.
16	
17	1. The core language: “APL for tensors”
18	
19	The core should remain recognizably APL.
20	
21	That matters because your current sw-apl already gives you the hard parts: a clean-room Rust interpreter, genuine glyph syntax, right-to-left evaluation, arbitrary-rank arrays, a browser implementation, Espanso/Emacs input, workspaces, and regression/conformance infrastructure. Its main historical limitation for this experiment is intentional: it models APL\360 / 5100-era APL rather than APL2, so it currently has flat arrays, no nesting, and no Each.
22	
23	By contrast, sw-cor24-apl has already explored exactly two features that become important here: nested/boxed arrays and Each, while retaining a right-to-left recursive-descent parser.
24	
25	That suggests:
26	
27	Do not mutate historical sw-apl into ML-APL. Fork the semantic architecture and create a new language mode/project.
28	
29	Call the research language M, L, or APLML; keep sw-apl historically disciplined.
30	
31	My preference for the actual language name is M.
32	
33	It fits the Iverson-family tradition:
34	
35	A → J → K → … → M
36	
37	and “M” can quietly stand for Machine, Model, Matrix, or ML, without making the language name cumbersome.
38	
39	APLML would be the better descriptive repo name initially, though:
40	
41	sw-aplml
42	
43	with:
44	
45	Language: M
46	Tagline: an array language for machine learning
47	
48	That avoids trying to own an unsearchable one-letter repository.
49	
50	2. Don't make relu, softmax, etc. merely funny spellings
51	
52	This is the most important design decision.
53	
54	Something like:
55	
56	Y ← relu W+.×X
57	
58	becoming:
59	
60	Y ← ♢ W+.×X
61	
62	doesn't really create a new language. It saves characters.
63	
64	Instead, ML primitives should exploit APL-level semantics.
65	
66	For example, classic APL already gives you a concise linear layer:
67	
68	B + W +.× X
69	
70	depending on axis convention.
71	
72	So Linear does not necessarily deserve a primitive glyph at all. Its value is primarily as a parameterized/model object, not as a mathematical operator.
73	
74	Likewise ReLU is already conceptually:
75	
76	0⌈X
77	
78	and sigmoid can be defined compositionally.
79	
80	This gives you a useful rule:
81	
82	A primitive earns a glyph only if it introduces a useful semantic concept that is awkward to express compositionally.
83	
84	For example:
85	
86	Concept	Existing array expression	New primitive justified?
87	ReLU	0⌈X	probably no
88	sigmoid	simple composition	probably no
89	softmax	possible but verbose + numerically subtle	yes
90	matmul	+.×	no
91	convolution	awkward axis/window expression	yes
92	gradient	impossible as ordinary array primitive	yes
93	loss	could be library function	maybe
94	optimizer step	stateful structural transform	yes
95	attention	composition of common ops	maybe library first
96	stop-gradient	new AD semantics	yes
97	parameter	new semantic category	yes
98	trainable model	structured value	yes

100	So rather than inventing twenty pictograms for PyTorch functions, create a small ML glyph vocabulary.
101	
102	3. A proposed ML glyph vocabulary
103	
104	Unicode already contains a very large mathematical operator repertoire, but Unicode explicitly does not assign unique semantics to every mathematical use; applications/languages decide those meanings in context.
105	
106	That means you can use existing Unicode characters rather than inventing a custom font.
107	
108	I would begin with about six new semantic primitives.
109	
110	Glyph	Spoken form	Meaning
111	∇	grad	derivative / gradient
112	⨂	tensor	tensor/outer interaction, if not conflicting with APL outer product
113	⧉	window	sliding window / convolution operand
114	⌁	soft	normalize logits / softmax-like transform
115	⚿ or another safe glyph	param	trainable parameter
116	↻	step	optimizer state transition

121	
122	∇
123	
124	because ML users already understand it.
125	
126	Example:
127	
128	G ← ∇ Loss Params
129	
130	or, preserving stronger APL dyadic structure:
131	
132	Params ∇ Loss
133

135	
136	∇Loss Params
137	
138	meaning:
139	
140	derive the gradient function of Loss, then apply it to Params.
141	
142	That is much more Iversonian.

145	
146	This is where the language could become genuinely distinctive.
147	
148	APL's superpower isn't merely arrays. It is that functions can be transformed by operators.
149	
150	Machine learning is full of function transformations:
151	
152	differentiate a function
153	vectorize a function
154	batch a function
155	checkpoint a function
156	jit/compile a function
157	map over devices
158	calculate value-and-gradient

173

176	Each, already familiar from modern APL

320	8. Mathematical binders should be first-class compiler constructs
321	
322	Sums and products are not merely glyphs.

324	This:
325	
326	$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i $$
327	
328	contains:
329	
330	operator      Σ
331	binder        i
332	lower bound   1
333	upper bound   n
334	body          x_i

337	
338	Reduce {
339	    op: Sum,
340	    variable: i,
341	    domain: Range(1,n),
342	    expr: x[i],
343	}

345	Then perform an arrayification pass.

347	If i indexes the only axis of x:
348	
349	Σᵢ xᵢ
350	
351	becomes:
352	
353	+/X
354	
355	For:
356	
357	$$ y_i = \sum_j W_{ij}x_j $$

359	the compiler can recognize contraction:
360	
361	contract axis j
362	
363	and lower to an inner product / matrix-vector operation.

365	This would be an outstanding feature because users could see:
366	
367	loops → indexed mathematics → contractions → array combinators

369	which is essentially the conceptual bridge between conventional ML notation and APL.

399	10. Tuples: yes—but don't confuse tuples with nested arrays
400	
401	Your secondary question deserves a firm distinction.
402	
403	APL2 already provides extremely powerful recursive heterogeneous structure: nested arrays may contain arrays of differing shape, rank, depth, and type.
404	
405	So this:
406	
407	(Weights Bias)
408	
409	can already conceptually be represented as a nested array.
410	
411	But a tuple should convey something different:
412	
413	fixed-position product structure whose elements do not participate in ordinary array scalar extension/broadcasting as one homogeneous array.
414	
415	For ML this matters greatly.
416	
417	A layer may return:
418	
419	(output, state)
420	
421	An optimizer step may return:
422	
423	(params, optimizer-state)
424	
425	A training iteration might yield:
426	
427	(loss, params, metrics)
428	
429	Treating those as an ordinary nested vector is semantically weak.
430	
431	So I would have three fundamental structural categories:
432	
433	Scalar
434	Array
435	Tuple
436	
437	with arrays recursively allowed to contain boxed/nested values if desired.

462	array	many things of the same structural axis space

given my APL-related work: 
sw-vibe-coding/sw-apl , 
sw-embed/sw-cor24-apl, 
sw-embed/web-sw-cor24-apl, and https://mlpl.softwarewrighter.com/ -- I'd like to consider a new approach to the intersection of APL and ML.  So imagine an APL2-inspired language (glyphs, right to left) that has ML primitives, new glyphs.  One approach would be to parse actual math expressions, which can be multi-line, with the notations above and below sums and products.  See also 
sw-vibe-coding/DiscoveryOne for ideas about parsing Espanso multiline expressions.  (secondary idea: how do tuples as first class language items fit in with an APL-like array language?).   I'm thinking of something like APLML (A Programming Language for Machine Learning) or just M or L in the style of A, J, K.    Also, there could be unicode-based glyphs for ML built-ins in sw-MLPL, like adam, relu, softmax, linear, sigmoid, etc.  --- With espanso, an escaped key stroke could produce a glyph and a smart editor could annotate glyphs with tooltips.  Help me come up with a design and plan for this idea.

You’re describing something more interesting than “APL with a few neural-network functions.” The coherent version is a new array language whose notation deliberately sits between APL and mathematical ML notation:

APL-style right-to-left evaluation and array semantics.
APL2-style nested arrays as the basis for structured data.
ML primitives that operate on whole tensors/models/parameter structures.
A second, spatial mathematical surface syntax for expressions such as sums, products, gradients, losses, and indexed tensor equations.
Tooling that makes glyph entry practical rather than nostalgic.

I would separate the idea into three layers, because trying to solve all of them in one grammar would likely make the language incoherent.

1. The core language: “APL for tensors”

The core should remain recognizably APL.

That matters because your current sw-apl already gives you the hard parts: a clean-room Rust interpreter, genuine glyph syntax, right-to-left evaluation, arbitrary-rank arrays, a browser implementation, Espanso/Emacs input, workspaces, and regression/conformance infrastructure. Its main historical limitation for this experiment is intentional: it models APL\360 / 5100-era APL rather than APL2, so it currently has flat arrays, no nesting, and no Each.

By contrast, sw-cor24-apl has already explored exactly two features that become important here: nested/boxed arrays and Each, while retaining a right-to-left recursive-descent parser.

That suggests:

Do not mutate historical sw-apl into ML-APL. Fork the semantic architecture and create a new language mode/project.

Call the research language M, L, or APLML; keep sw-apl historically disciplined.

My preference for the actual language name is M.

It fits the Iverson-family tradition:

A → J → K → … → M

and “M” can quietly stand for Machine, Model, Matrix, or ML, without making the language name cumbersome.

APLML would be the better descriptive repo name initially, though:

sw-aplml

with:

Language: M
Tagline: an array language for machine learning

That avoids trying to own an unsearchable one-letter repository.

2. Don't make relu, softmax, etc. merely funny spellings

This is the most important design decision.

Something like:

Y ← relu W+.×X

becoming:

Y ← ♢ W+.×X

doesn't really create a new language. It saves characters.

Instead, ML primitives should exploit APL-level semantics.

For example, classic APL already gives you a concise linear layer:

B + W +.× X

depending on axis convention.

So Linear does not necessarily deserve a primitive glyph at all. Its value is primarily as a parameterized/model object, not as a mathematical operator.

Likewise ReLU is already conceptually:

0⌈X

and sigmoid can be defined compositionally.

This gives you a useful rule:

A primitive earns a glyph only if it introduces a useful semantic concept that is awkward to express compositionally.

For example:

Concept	Existing array expression	New primitive justified?
ReLU	0⌈X	probably no
sigmoid	simple composition	probably no
softmax	possible but verbose + numerically subtle	yes
matmul	+.×	no
convolution	awkward axis/window expression	yes
gradient	impossible as ordinary array primitive	yes
loss	could be library function	maybe
optimizer step	stateful structural transform	yes
attention	composition of common ops	maybe library first
stop-gradient	new AD semantics	yes
parameter	new semantic category	yes
trainable model	structured value	yes

So rather than inventing twenty pictograms for PyTorch functions, create a small ML glyph vocabulary.

3. A proposed ML glyph vocabulary

Unicode already contains a very large mathematical operator repertoire, but Unicode explicitly does not assign unique semantics to every mathematical use; applications/languages decide those meanings in context.

That means you can use existing Unicode characters rather than inventing a custom font.

I would begin with about six new semantic primitives.

Glyph	Spoken form	Meaning
∇	grad	derivative / gradient
⨂	tensor	tensor/outer interaction, if not conflicting with APL outer product
⧉	window	sliding window / convolution operand
⌁	soft	normalize logits / softmax-like transform
⚿ or another safe glyph	param	trainable parameter
↻	step	optimizer state transition

I'm intentionally not strongly endorsing those exact glyphs yet. Glyph selection should come after the semantic inventory, because visually clever symbols become regrettable language syntax.

One especially good candidate is:

∇

because ML users already understand it.

Example:

G ← ∇ Loss Params

or, preserving stronger APL dyadic structure:

Params ∇ Loss

But I would actually treat ∇ as an operator, not a function:

∇Loss Params

meaning:

derive the gradient function of Loss, then apply it to Params.

That is much more Iversonian.

4. Operators are probably more important than new functions

This is where the language could become genuinely distinctive.

APL's superpower isn't merely arrays. It is that functions can be transformed by operators.

Machine learning is full of function transformations:

differentiate a function
vectorize a function
batch a function
checkpoint a function
jit/compile a function
map over devices
calculate value-and-gradient
attach trainable parameters
freeze part of a model

These map beautifully onto the APL operator concept.

For example, conceptually:

∇F

gradient of F

⌸F

batched/vectorized F

F¨

Each, already familiar from modern APL

F⍤R

rank-sensitive application

and potentially:

F⍢

training/update transformation

So an optimizer might not be:

adam(model, gradients)

but:

Params ← Rate Adam Loss Params

or even an operator-derived training verb:

Train ← Adam⍤Loss
Params ← Train Params Batch

The exact notation needs experimentation, but this direction is stronger than assigning Adam a decorative Unicode glyph.

5. The real breakthrough: make mathematical notation another surface syntax

Your multiline idea is potentially the differentiator.

Don't try to force two-dimensional mathematics directly into the ordinary APL lexer.

Instead build:

          ┌─────────────┐
APL glyph │             │
source ──▶│             │
          │ semantic IR │──▶ evaluator
Math 2D ─▶│             │
source    │             │
          └─────────────┘

APL syntax and mathematical notation are then two parsers for one expression IR.

That is very similar philosophically to what web-sw-cor24-apl already does in the other direction: it can display the same operations as representative ASCII words, APL glyphs, or literate descriptions.

You would extend that idea from display aliases to actual bidirectional notation.

6. Do not encode 2-D math as fake lines of text

For example, this:

$$ \operatorname{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}} {\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}} $$

cannot robustly be represented by counting spaces in:

              e^zᵢ
    ----------------------
        K
        Σ     e^zⱼ
       j=1

unless the editor owns the layout.

Unicode itself distinguishes between character encoding and higher-level mathematical composition; MathML/TeX-like systems provide structure that plain Unicode doesn't.

So I would borrow the best DiscoveryOne idea:

position is syntax, but serialize position explicitly.

DiscoveryOne already proposes source objects with (x,y,z) coordinates and semantic facets. You only need (x,y) for mathematics.

Internally:

struct MathGlyph {
    text: String,
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

but very quickly parse those into structural nodes:

Fraction
 ├─ numerator
 │   └─ Exp(Index(z,i))
 └─ denominator
     └─ Sum
         ├─ binder: j
         ├─ lower: 1
         ├─ upper: K
         └─ Exp(Index(z,j))

That becomes:

Expr::Div(
    Exp(Index(z,i)),
    Reduce {
        op: Add,
        binder: j,
        range: 1..K,
        body: Exp(Index(z,j))
    }
)

And then lower it to APL-array semantics.

That separation is crucial.

7. Math notation → array algebra should be visible

This would make an excellent teaching/research environment.

Input:

$$ y_i = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}} $$

Compiler interpretation:

index notation
      ↓
axis semantics
      ↓
array algebra
      ↓
M/APL source

For example, conceptually:

E ← * X - ⌈/X
Y ← E ÷ +/E

The user could switch among:

paper math
indexed math AST
APL/M expression
shape trace
evaluated arrays

That dovetails extremely well with what you're doing in MLPL and the “learn visually” direction.

And it gives the project an educational purpose larger than “APL with ML built-ins.”

8. Mathematical binders should be first-class compiler constructs

Sums and products are not merely glyphs.

This:

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i $$

contains:

operator      Σ
binder        i
lower bound   1
upper bound   n
body          x_i

So parse it initially as:

Reduce {
    op: Sum,
    variable: i,
    domain: Range(1,n),
    expr: x[i],
}

Then perform an arrayification pass.

If i indexes the only axis of x:

Σᵢ xᵢ

becomes:

+/X

For:

$$ y_i = \sum_j W_{ij}x_j $$

the compiler can recognize contraction:

contract axis j

and lower to an inner product / matrix-vector operation.

This would be an outstanding feature because users could see:

loops → indexed mathematics → contractions → array combinators

which is essentially the conceptual bridge between conventional ML notation and APL.

9. Add Einstein notation before adding dozens of ML built-ins

I'd prioritize this surprisingly highly.

For example:

$$ C_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik} B_{kj} $$

should become something structurally equivalent to:

C ← A +.× B

Likewise common tensor contractions could be inferred from repeated bound indices.

That means your language has something resembling:

math compiler
    ↓
index contraction
    ↓
APL array algebra

This is much more interesting than:

matmul(A,B)

And it fits your previous work translating CNN formulas to MLPL exceptionally well.

10. Tuples: yes—but don't confuse tuples with nested arrays

Your secondary question deserves a firm distinction.

APL2 already provides extremely powerful recursive heterogeneous structure: nested arrays may contain arrays of differing shape, rank, depth, and type.

So this:

(Weights Bias)

can already conceptually be represented as a nested array.

But a tuple should convey something different:

fixed-position product structure whose elements do not participate in ordinary array scalar extension/broadcasting as one homogeneous array.

For ML this matters greatly.

A layer may return:

(output, state)

An optimizer step may return:

(params, optimizer-state)

A training iteration might yield:

(loss, params, metrics)

Treating those as an ordinary nested vector is semantically weak.

So I would have three fundamental structural categories:

Scalar
Array
Tuple

with arrays recursively allowed to contain boxed/nested values if desired.

11. Make tuples named products, inspired by DiscoveryOne/Tuplet

DiscoveryOne's ancestry is relevant because Tuplet/DiscoveryOne treats named tuples and multi-output verbs as fundamental.

For M, I would simplify the idea.

For example:

R ← ⟨Loss Params Metrics⟩

or constructor syntax:

⟨loss: L, params: P, metrics: M⟩

and selection:

R.loss

You don't need to force tuple semantics into APL indexing.

The semantic distinction becomes:

Structure	Meaning
array	many things of the same structural axis space
nested array	array whose cells may themselves be arrays/objects
tuple	one product value consisting of distinct roles
named tuple	tuple with semantic fields

That distinction is extremely useful for ML.

Consider Adam state:

AdamState =
    ⟨step,
      first_moment,
      second_moment⟩

Those values are structurally related but are not an array.

12. Tuples solve a longstanding awkwardness in array languages

APL is excellent when one answer is an array.

Modern computation often wants multiple semantically different outputs.

Instead of conventions such as:

2⊃R

you could have:

R.params
R.loss

or destructuring:

⟨L P S⟩ ← Train Batch State

This would fit right-to-left evaluation nicely:

⟨Loss Params State⟩ ← Batch Train State

A function can remain conceptually monadic/dyadic yet return a product.

This is one place where I think departing from traditional APL is worth it.

13. A tentative core type model

I would avoid a traditional static type system initially.

Instead introduce structural runtime categories plus optional shape annotations:

Value
├── Scalar
│   ├── Int
│   ├── Float
│   ├── Complex
│   ├── Bool
│   └── Char
│
├── Array
│   ├── Shape
│   ├── Element storage
│   └── Rank
│
├── Box/Nested
│
├── Tuple
│   ├── positional
│   └── named
│
├── Function
│
└── Model/Parameter

Eventually:

Tensor[F32; B,H,W,C]

could exist as compiler metadata without infecting normal APL syntax.

14. Shape should be part of the language's explanatory model

APL already makes shape fundamental through ⍴.

ML should take that further.

For example a smart editor could show:

Y ← W +.× X

with hover metadata:

W : 768 × 3072
X : 3072 × 128
────────────────
Y : 768 × 128

And math notation:

$$ Y_{ij}=\sum_k W_{ik}X_{kj} $$

could annotate:

i → 768
j → 128
k → 3072 (contracted)

This may be more valuable pedagogically than the ML glyphs themselves.

15. The editor is part of the language

APL historically required specialized input.

You've already solved much of that problem in sw-apl: the browser has an APL keyboard, and the project explicitly supports Espanso and Emacs keymaps.

For M I would make this a first-class design principle:

Source remains Unicode text, but editing is mnemonic.

Example Espanso mappings:

\grad     → ∇
\rho      → ⍴
\iota     → ⍳
\each     → ¨
\sum      → ∑
\product  → ∏
\alpha    → α
\partial  → ∂

Maybe use an APL-style prefix key:

Alt-G G   → ∇
Alt-G R   → ⍴

but Espanso provides the portable baseline.

The editor should then display:

∇
Gradient operator
Derives a function computing ∂output/∂argument

on hover.

That largely eliminates the classic “APL hieroglyphics” objection.

16. Make glyphs readable without changing source

Borrow directly from web-sw-cor24-apl.

It already supports:

representative syntax
APL glyph syntax
literate syntax

Extend that to four synchronized views:

Glyph
    ∇Loss P

Mnemonic
    grad Loss P

Literate
    gradient-of Loss applied-to P

Mathematical
       ∂ Loss
    ─────────
       ∂ P

All four views point at the same AST.

That is a much stronger UI than a syntax highlighter.

17. Don't parse arbitrary printed mathematics in M0

There is a large difference between:

“our editor understands structured two-dimensional math”

and:

“paste arbitrary mathematics from a paper and we'll parse it.”

The latter rapidly becomes an OCR/TeX/CAS research project.

For the first version, constrain the grammar to:

fractions
superscripts
subscripts
Σ
Π
∂
∇
parentheses/brackets
indexed variables
equality
common arithmetic
perhaps expectation E
tensor contractions

That is enough for a surprisingly large fraction of introductory ML equations.

Softmax alone is a good proof:

$$ \sigma_i(z)=\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}} $$

Google's ML material uses essentially this standard formula.

18. The first demonstration should be softmax

It exercises nearly everything you care about.

Start with the paper notation:

$$ s_i = \frac{e^{z_i}} {\sum_j e^{z_j}} $$

Then show its interpretation:

numerator
    exponent(index(z,i))

denominator
    reduce(add, j, exponent(index(z,j)))

Then arrayify:

E ← *Z
S ← E ÷ +/E

Then stabilized version:

E ← *Z-⌈/Z
S ← E÷+/E

Then replace the implementation with a primitive if desired:

S ← ⌁Z

Clicking ⌁ could expand back into its definition.

That gives you a beautiful distinction between:

primitive as abstraction

and

array expression as explanation

19. Second demo: a linear layer should deliberately have no glyph

Math:

$$ y = Wx+b $$

M:

Y ← B + W +.× X

This demonstrates the opposite lesson:

APL already is an ML notation when the operation is fundamentally array algebra.

That's important intellectually. Otherwise the project risks seeming like a Unicode façade over a tensor library.

20. Third demo: gradient descent

Math:

$$ \theta_{t+1} = \theta_t-\eta\nabla_\theta L(\theta_t) $$

M might look like:

Θ ← Θ - η × ∇Loss Θ

That is where the ML extension pays for itself.

And then:

Train ← {
    Θ ← Θ - η × ∇Loss Θ
}

or an eventual derived optimizer form.

21. Fourth demo: Adam shows why tuples matter

Adam has:

parameters
first moment
second moment
step
hyperparameters

So something like:

State ← ⟨step:0 m:0×Θ v:0×Θ⟩

then:

⟨Θ State⟩ ← Grad AdamStep ⟨Θ State⟩

This makes the tuple work clearly justified rather than an arbitrary language feature.

22. Fifth demo: CNN equation → array operation

Use one of the nested-sum convolution equations you've been exploring.

Something like:

$$ Y_{i,j,k} = \sum_m\sum_n\sum_c X_{i+m,j+n,c}K_{m,n,c,k} $$

Your math parser recognizes:

free indices:      i j k
contracted:        m n c

and lowers it to:

window + contraction

Then either:

Y ← K Conv X

or a composition of window and inner-product primitives.

This would connect directly to the CNN/math work in MLPL.

If ∇ is going to mean anything beyond symbolic rewriting, every primitive eventually needs derivative metadata.

That registry could be the heart of the language.

26. I'd make primitives declarative

For example, conceptually:

content.content:
set shell := ["sh", "-cu"]

# Show available repository tasks.
default:
    @just --list

# Talk to demo 01: `just chat "my mom never listens to me"`. Loads the committed weights.
chat text:
    @./scripts/run-chat "{{text}}"

# Run the committed demo transcript through demo 01, one turn per line.
transcript:
    @./scripts/run-chat < demos/eliza/transcript.txt

# Serve the browser demo locally with live rebuild at http://127.0.0.1:8080/.
web:
    cd crates/tdm-web && trunk serve --open

# Re-export every literate document under docs/literate/ to its published HTML (Emacs, batch, nothing evaluated).
literate:
    ./scripts/publish-literate

# Check every literate document: tangle parity, primer results, and a fresh export.
tangle:
    ./scripts/check-tangle

# Build the live demo into pages/ (committed; the Pages workflow publishes it as is).
site:
    ./scripts/build-site

# Serve the built pages/ directory at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ exactly as Pages will.
serve-site:
    cd pages && python3 -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1

# Re-export demo 01's trained model as the JSON bundle the browser embeds.
eliza-export:
    ../sw-mlpl/target/release/mlpl-repl --source-dir . -f demos/eliza/export.mlpl

# Featurize demo 01's oracle corpus for model 4 (Rust; writes tmp/model4/data.json).
model4-featurize:
    mkdir -p tmp/model4
    cargo run --release -p eliza-sim --bin featurize -- demos/eliza/oracle/corpus.tsv demos/eliza/oracle/frame-nouls.tsv demos/eliza/probe-labels.tsv demos/eliza/probe-nouls.tsv fixtures/bundles/demo01-doctor.json tmp/model4/data.json

# Train model 4 on the featurized corpus and rewrite its bundle (about 11 minutes).
model4-train: model4-featurize
    ../sw-mlpl/target/release/mlpl-repl --source-dir . -f demos/eliza/v4/export.mlpl

# Score model 4 against the oracle: agreement, per rule, calibration, policy.
model4-score:
    cargo run --release -p eliza-sim --example oracle_score

# Rewrite the Noul labels of the generated sentences (demos/eliza/oracle/frame-nouls.tsv).
model4-frame-nouls:
    ../sw-mlpl/target/release/mlpl-repl --source-dir . -f demos/eliza/v4/frame-nouls.mlpl

# Build the (state, question, choices, answer) tuples for the PR05 card scorer.
scorer-cards:
    mkdir -p tmp/model5
    cargo run --release -p eliza-sim --bin cards -- demos/eliza/oracle/corpus.tsv demos/eliza/oracle/frame-nouls.tsv fixtures/bundles/demo01-doctor.json tmp/model5/data.json

# Train the PR05 card scorer and rewrite its bundle (about 6 minutes).
scorer-train: scorer-cards
    ../sw-mlpl/target/release/mlpl-repl --source-dir . -f demos/eliza/v5/export.mlpl

# Score the card scorer against model 4's fixed head, including on cards held out of training.
scorer-score:
    cargo run --release -p eliza-sim --example scorer_score

# Train demo 01's Choice model and rewrite its weights (about 25 seconds).
eliza-train:
    ./scripts/run-eliza-train

# Score local LLMs on the same held-out messages, by the same bounded-choice method (needs ollama).
llm-baseline:
    ./scripts/llm-baseline

# Run the concise hello: the short annotated program, over the corpus it is given.
concise-hello:
    ../sw-mlpl/target/release/mlpl-repl --source-dir . -f demos/typed-decisions/concise-hello.mlpl -- demos/typed-decisions/messages.json

# Run the hello-world typed-decision demo (about three seconds).
typed-decisions:
    ../sw-mlpl/target/release/mlpl-repl --source-dir . -f demos/typed-decisions/typed-decisions.mlpl

# Bundle the in-browser training program and run it standalone, as the gate does.
browser-program:
    ./scripts/check-browser-program

# The full pre-commit gate: structure, boundaries, links, catalog, style, tests, probes.
check:
    ./scripts/check

# Run native mlplunit tests; arguments select paths, tags, or filters.
tests *args:
    ./scripts/run-tests {{args}}

# Re-run the upstream-finding reproducers and require the documented outcome.
probes:
    ./scripts/run-probes

# Check canonical formatting and the module-purpose comment on tracked MLPL source.
mlpl-style:
    ./scripts/check-mlpl-style

# Check that no demo vocabulary has leaked into lib/, crates/, or schemas/.
abstraction:
    ./scripts/check-abstraction

# Check that every catalog entry names files that exist.
catalog:
    ./scripts/check-catalog

# Check that every relative documentation link resolves.
doc-links:
    ./scripts/check-doc-links

# Rust gate for the microscope crates: formatting, pedantic clippy, and tests.
rust:
    ./scripts/check-rust

# Validate every committed decision trace against decision-trace-v1.
traces:
    ./scripts/check-traces

members = ["crates/tdm-trace", "crates/tdm-model", "crates/tdm-web", "demos/eliza/sim"]
resolver = "2"

[workspace.lints.rust]
